problem: Multimodal visual navigation suffers from insufficient fusion of RGB, depth and semantic cues, weak target constraints, and action decisions that are easily disturbed by partial occlusion in complex scenes.
motivation: Single-image features cannot stably represent obstacles, target positions and traversable areas, and unconstrained multimodal fusion adds redundancy. The paper uses a target-conditioned task token to steer attention across modalities, and adds memory and safety filtering to make decisions stable and collision-free.
key_idea: Use a task token as the query in cross-modal Transformer attention over RGB, depth and semantic tokens, feed the fused features through a GRU scene memory to an RL policy, and filter actions with explicit safety constraints.
insight: The ablations (Figure 3, text only) show every component helps. Removing the task token, memory or safety constraints lowers success to 91.0%, 90.4% and 92.1%, and RGB-only input drops to 88.7% success and 0.702 SPL. Removing safety constraints raises the collision rate from 3.7% to 8.6%, so the safety filter mainly cuts collisions. The evidence is weak: it comes from a small custom dataset with no public benchmark or standard baselines.
method: Multimodal state input: RGB, depth, semantic labels, target direction vector and local position are size-aligned, normalized and timestamp-matched into a state vector s_t.
Modal embedding + position encoding: lightweight conv encoders and linear maps project each modality to tokens; 2D spatial position encoding and modality-type encoding are added.

Task-token cross-modal attention: the task token (target, direction, distance change) is the query over RGB/depth/semantic tokens; softmax weights aggregate value-projected tokens into a fused feature h_t.
Local scene memory: a GRU takes [h_t; a_{t-1}; p_t] to update memory m_t, and a sigmoid layer over [h_t; m_t; g_t] gives the state o_t.

RL policy: the policy outputs probabilities over forward, left, right, stop and obstacle-avoidance adjustment. The reward is goal-distance reduction minus collision and path-length cost plus arrival reward, and the objective is the discounted return.
Safety-constrained action selection: choose the argmax-probability action among those whose predicted obstacle distance is at least D_safe and whose goal-direction deviation is at most E_max.

setting.backbone: Task-driven Transformer + GRU memory + RL policy network (trained from scratch, lightweight conv encoders)
setting.training_data: Self-collected data from 36 indoor navigation scenes: 1,280 valid trajectories, 92,400 state transitions (64,680 train / 13,860 val / 13,860 test); AdamW, batch 32, 100 epochs
setting.observation: RGB 224x224, depth 224x224, semantic labels 224x224, target vector, local position state
setting.action_space: Discrete: forward, left turn, right turn, stop, obstacle-avoidance adjustment
setting.simulator: Not specified (36 indoor navigation scenes, simulator unnamed)
setting.privileged: Semantic labels and the target direction/relative-distance vector are provided as input (likely ground truth); A* baseline used the scene raster map

numbers.eval_set_note: 192 complete test trajectories drawn from the paper's own test split
numbers.extra: Trained on the authors' own 36-scene dataset; semantic labels and target vector used as input
numbers.evidence: Table 3. Performance comparison of different visual navigation algorithms: Proposed Method 94.8 / 0.801 / 15.4 / 3.7 / 32.6

numbers.bench: other:Custom indoor navigation, unseen complex scenes
numbers.eval_set_note: 12 unseen indoor scenes, 240 trajectories (narrow passages, target occlusion, continuous corners, dense obstacles)
numbers.evidence: In unseen scenes, the model still maintains 91.6% success rate and 4.9% collision rate.

numbers_note: Ablation and generalization results are in Figure 3, which is a figure; only the values quoted in the text are captured. No standard benchmark is used.
results: On the authors' own indoor dataset, the method reaches 94.8% SR, 0.801 SPL and 3.7% collision rate. The strongest baseline, an ordinary Transformer, gets 91.2% SR, 0.742 SPL and 6.9% collisions. On 12 unseen scenes it keeps 91.6% SR.
limitations: Evaluated only on a small self-built dataset with an unnamed simulator; no standard benchmarks (Habitat, etc.) and no comparison to published navigation methods.
Baselines are generic (A*, DQN, PPO, plain Transformer), and the setup relies on semantic labels and target vectors as input, which may be privileged.
No real-robot tests; dynamic obstacles and lightweight deployment are left as future work, and latency is the highest of all compared methods (32.6 ms).
